INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Tenth Report on the Demands for Grants (2004-05) relating to the
Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region.
2. The Committee heard the presentation of the Secretary of the Ministry in its sitting held on
10 August, 2004.
3. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has mainly relied upon the
following:—
(i) Presentation made by the Secretary of the Ministry;
(ii) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the year 2004-05;
(iii) Explanatory Notes on the Demands for Grants (2004-05) received from the Ministry;
(iv) Annual Report of the Ministry for the year 2003-04;
(v) Written replies furnished by the Ministry to the Questionnaires sent to it by the
Secretariat; and
(vi) Oral and written clarifications to the points/issues raised by the Members in the
meetings of the Committee.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its sitting held on 18 August, 2004.
5. For the facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
SUSHMA SWARAJ

come under the purview of the Ministry of Home Affairs. However, this time besides considering the Demands for
Grants for 2005-06, the Committee has decided to give special focus to “Disaster Management” in this Report as this
subject has been transferred to the Ministry of Home Affairs from the Ministry of Agriculture in 2002 and also keeping
in view the havoc and devastation caused by Tsunami not only in India but in many of its neighbouring Asian countries
on 26th December, 2004. The Tsunami tragedy was followed by unprecedented snowfall in Jammu & Kashmir in early
2005 causing extreme difficulties to the residents of the State and other people. The Committee has therefore devoted an
exclusive chapter (Chapter-IV) to this subject so as to highlight the significance and importance of Disaster
Management The Committee, besides having the presentation of Home Secretary on the subject also heard experts viz.

2:         Under Rule 272 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States, during the Budget
Session after the general discussion on the Budget in the Houses is over and the Houses are adjourned for a fixed period,
the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees are mandated to consider the Demands for Grants of the
related Ministries during the said recess period of Parliament and make reports thereon to the Houses within the specific
period. But in view of the rescheduling of the Budget Session (2006), a decision was taken to conclude the entire
financial business before the Houses adjourned for the Budget recess and Rule 272 was suspended in its application to
consideration of Demands for Grants 
(2006-07) of the related Ministries/Departments by Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, by a
Motion moved by the Minister of State  in the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs in the Rajya Sabha on March 18, 2006
which was adopted by the House on the same day. Notwithstanding discussion and voting on the Demands for Grants of
the respective Ministries/Departments for the year 2006-07 by the Lok Sabha, during the first part of the Budget
Session, it was decided by the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha and Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha that the Department-
related Parliamentary Standing Committees will examine the Demands for Grants and present their reports thereon to
the respective Houses.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One-Hundred and Twenty Sixth Report on the Demands for Grants (2007-08) relating
to the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).
2. While examining Demands for Grants every year it has been the practice in this Committee
to take up one subject/issue for its special focus. It had taken “Disaster Management” and “Delhi
Police and its functioning” for its special focus during 2005-06 and 2006-07, respectively. During
the year 2007-08, the Committee has identified “Union Territories (UTs) without Legislatures” as
the focus area in this report. The Committee has also taken up a separate subject of
“Administration of UTs” for a detailed study and has already presented a report on Administration
of UTs of Chandigarh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Pondicherry. It is in the process of
studying the other UTs. During its visit to the UTs without legislature, the Administrators have
brought to the notice of the Committee that though they are contributing substantially by way of
tax collection to the Exchequer, but the budgetary allocation to them is not commensurate to their
contribution. As a result their development/projects are hampered. To facilitate in-depth examination
of the subject by the Committee the officials of the Home Ministry had made an exclusive
presentation in the matter before it. During that presentation, the Chief Secretary/Administrators of
Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu and
Lakshadweep were present.

PREFACE
I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Thirty second Report on Demands for Grants (2008-09) relating to
the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).
2. While examining Demands for Grants every year, it has been the practice in this Committee
to take up one subject/issue for special focus. It had earlier taken up “Disaster Management”,
“Delhi Police and its functioning” and “Union Territories without Legislature” focused study during
2005-06, 2006-07 and 2007-08, respectively. In the current year, the Committee had decided to
highlight “Naxalism” in its report. To facilitate in-depth examination of the subject by the
Committee, the officials of the Home Ministry made an exclusive presentation in the matter before
it. However, keeping in view the wide ranging implications of the subject, the Committee decided
to make a detailed study of the subject and present a separate report after taking into account the
views of the affected State Governments.
3. The Committee held in all three sittings to complete the examination of Demands for Grants
of the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Committee heard the Home Secretary on Demands for Grants
(2008-09) of Ministry of Home Affairs and Naxalism in its meetings held on 28th March and 5th
April, 2008, respectively.

PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Fifty-seventh Report on the Arms (Amendment) Bill, 2011.
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred
♣ the Arms (Amendment) Bill, 2011
(Annexure-I) as introduced on 12 th December, 2011 in the Rajya Sabha and pending therein, to the
Committee on 13 th January, 2012, for examination and report by 31 st March, 2012.
3. The Bill seeks to amend sub-section 3 of Section 27 of the Arms Act, 1959 by substituting
the words “shall be punishable with death”, with the words “shall be punishable with death or
imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine” in the said sub-section.
4. The Committee considered the Arms (Amendment) Bill, 2011 in its sitting held on
6
th February, 2012, and also heard the presentation of the representatives of the Ministry of Home
Affairs on the Bill. As per practice, senior officers of the Legislative Department and the
Department of Legal Affairs were also present in that sitting to respond to the queries of the
Members.
5. The Committee in its sitting held on 13
th March, 2012 considered and adopted this Report.
6. The report is based on the following documents:–
(i) The Arms (Amendment) Bill, 2011;
(ii) Detailed background Note on the Bill as received from the Ministry of Home Affairs;
(iii) The Arms Act, 1959;
(iv) Oral evidence tendered by the representatives of Ministry of Home Affairs, Law and
Justice; and
(v) Replies received from the Ministry of Home Affairs on the queries raised by the
Members.
7. For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
M. VENKA

REPORT 
I, the Chairman, Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee, present this Eighteenth Report relating to the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 
1995•. The Bill seeks to make special provisions for the prevention of, and for coping with 
terrorist and disruptive activities and to supplement the criminal law. 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred .. the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya 
Sabha on the 18th May, 1995 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and 
report within two days. 
3. Accordingly, the Committee considered the Bill in its meeting held on the 19th May, 
1995 and also heard the Home Secretary. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the report in its meeting held on the 22nd 
May, 1995. 
5. Some Members of the Committee gave amendments/suggestions on the Bill which 
are appended to the report. 
6. In his presentation, the Home Secretary stated that the following provisions under 
TADA which were either misused or had the potential of being misused are proposed to be 
dropped in the new legislation:-
(i) Section 5 of TADA Act makes unauthorised possession~f arms in a notified area 
an offence. The Arms Act provides for deterrent punishment for possession of 
certain classes of unauthorised arms. Therefore, there is no need to repeat the 
provision in the new legislation. 
(ii) Section 15 of T ADA Act provides that confessions made to a police officer are 
admissible in evidence. This is against the grain of the normal provision of the 
Indian Evidence Act, 1872 whereunder statements made to the police are not 
admissible as evidence. 
(iii) Section 21(1)(c) and (d) lays down certain presumptions relating to confessions. 
This section provides that if it is proved that one of the accused makes a confession 
that the other has committed the offence, it shall be presumed that the other 
(accused) has committed the offence. It also provides that if it is proved that an 
accused has made a confession to any person other than a police officer, it shall be 
presumed that he has committed such an offence. 
(iv) Section 20(8)(b) provides that a court shall not grant bail unless it is satisfied that

offence under T ADA. This provision made it extremely difficult to obtain bail in 
TADA cases.

Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred Eighty Second Report on the Rescue, Rehabilitation and
Reconstruction plan in the aftermath of the floods and landslides in Jammu and Kashmir.
2. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, in its
meeting held on 10th October, 2014, taking note of the unprecedented devastation caused by
rains and floods in Jammu and Kashmir, heard the presentation of the Home Secretary and
representatives of the Government of Jammu and Kashmir on the subject.
3. The Committee while finalizing its report, relied on the following papers/documents:-
(i) Background note furnished by the Ministry of Home Affairs; and
(ii) Replies to the queries of Members raised during its sittings.
4. The Committee in its sitting held on 4 th December, 2014 considered and adopted the
present report.
5. For facility of reference and convenience, Observations and Recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
P. BHATTACHARYA
Chairman,

REPORT 
I, the Chairman, Committee on Home Affairs, having bean authorised by the 
Committee, preSent this Nineteenth Report on the Representation of the People (Amend­
ment) Bill*, 1995. The Bill seeks to further amend the representation of the People Act, 
1950. 
2. In pursuan.ce of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred** the bill, as introduced in the Lok 
Sabha on the 20th March, 1995 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and 
report with the direction that the Committee may submit its report at the earliest so that the 
Bill could be passed during the current session of Parliament. 
3. Accordingly, the Committee met on the 31st May, 1995 to consider the Bill and 
adopt its report thereon. 
4. As per the Statement of Objects and Reasons given in the Bill amendment to the 
entries relating to the State of Kamataka in the Fourth Schedule to the Representation of 
the People Act, 1950, has been necessitated consequent upon the coming into force of the 
Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992 and the Constitution (Seventy-fourth 
Amendment) Act , 1992, and the amendment made in the law by the State of Kamataka 
relating to the local bodies. Under the amended law, the local bodies, namely, City 
Municipal Corporations, City Municipal Councils, Town Municipal Councils, Town Pancha­
yats, Zilla Panchayats, Taluk Panchayats, Gram Panchayats have been created. These local 
bodies will substitute the existing local bodies namely, Municipalities, Mandai Panchayats, 
Cantonment Board, Notified Area Committees and Zilla Parishads, except the Cantonment 
Boards for the purpose of election to the Legislative Council in Kamataka. 
5. In view of the above, the Committee is of the view that there is a need to amend the 
entries relating to the State of Kamataka in the Fourth Schedule to the Representation of 
the People Act, 1950. The Committee agrees with the proposed amendment and recom­
mends that the Bill be passed.

May 31, 1995

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, ·the Chairman of the Department-related Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been 
authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Second Report of the 
Committee. 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, 
the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha, !*referred the Governors 
(Emoluments, Allowances and Privileges) 2•• Amendment Bill, 1992, as introduced in the Lok Sabha 
on the 3rd March, 1992, and pending in that House, to the Committee for examination and report. 
3. The Committee, in its meet ing held on the lOth August, 1993 discussed the provisions of the Bill 
and took up clause-by-claus~ consideration thereof. 
4. The Committee, at its meeting held on the 16th August, 1993" consider ed and adopted the draft 
Report. 
5. In view of the decisions taken by the Government of India to the effect that the pension 
equivalent of gratuity may not be deducted while fixing the pay of re-employed pensioners , and that 
the pension equivalent of gratuity will not be taken into account while fixing the initial pay of retired 
Judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts appointed to Committees or on Commissions, it 
was felt that the benefit of not deducting pension equivalent of gratuity from the emolument s payable 
to Governors, may be allowed. According to the amendments proposed in the Bill, Governors who 
had received retirement gratuity in respect of previous service would be benefited . Accordingly, 
clause 2 of the Bill was adopted by the Committee without any change. 
6. Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted with some changes which are of a 
consequential or drafting nature. 
7. The Committee recommends that the Bill, as reported , be passed .

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman• of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee, present this Twentieth Report of the Committee on the Union Public Service 
Commission (UPSC). 
2. The Committee while discussing the Annual Report (1992-93) of the Ministry of 
Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (which is the administrative Ministry in respect of 
UPSC) noted that Parliament could not get time for the last several years to discuss the 
Reports of the UPSC. The Committee, therefore, decided in its sitting held on the 27th 
May, 1993, to examine the working of the UPSC in detail as part of the consideration of the 
Annual ~eport of the Ministry. 
3. The Committee while making its recommendations and observations has taken into 
consideration the following papers and !lubmissions/clarifications:-
(a) Annual Reports of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions for 
the years 1992-93 and 1993-94. 
(b) Annual Reports of the UPSC for the years 1988-89, 1989-90, 1990-91 and 1991-92. 
(c) Background note and replies to the Committee's Questionnaires as furnished by the 
Ministry and the UPSC. 
(d) Submissions made and clarifications given by the representatives of the Ministry and 
the UPSC before the Committee. 
4. The Committee completed its deliberations in six sittings. Relevant Minutes of the 
sittings of the Committee are appended to the Report. 
5. The Committee heard the Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and 
Pensions and the representatives of the UPSC on the subject in its sitting held on the 11th 
February, 1994. 
6. In its sitting held on the 26th' May, 1994, the Committee further discussed the subject 
and sought clarifications from the representatives of the Ministry and the UPSC. 
7. The Committe~ in its sitting held on the 19th July, 1994 sought further clarifications 
from the Secretary of the Ministry and the representatives of the UPSC and asked them to 
furnish information on certain points. 
8. In its sitting held on the 28th November, 1994, the Committee considered the 
information furnished by the Ministry and the UPSC. 
9. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its sitting held on the 13th June , 
1995.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs,
having been authorized by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, do hereby present this Two
Hundred Second Report on Demands for Grants (2017-18) relating to the Ministry of Development of
North Eastern Region (DoNER).
2. Under Rule 272 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States, the
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs is mandated to consider the
Demands for Grants of the related Ministries, and make report thereon. In pursuance thereof, the
Committee in its sitting held on 1st March, 2017 heard the presentation of the Secretary, and other
officials of the Ministry of DoNER as well as officers of the Implementing Ministries/Departments/
Agencies and considered the Demands for Grants (2017-18) of that Ministry.
3. The Committee considered and adopted the draft Report in its sitting held on 20th March, 2017.
4. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has relied mainly upon the following
papers received from the Ministry of DoNER:-
(i) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the year 2017-18;
(ii) Background Notes on the Demands for Grants (2017-18);
(iii) Outcome Budget (2017-18) of the Ministry;
(iv) Annual Report (2016-17) of the Ministry;
(v) Written replies furnished by the Ministry to the Questionnaires sent to it by the Committee;
(vi) Presentation made by the Secretary of the Ministry and oral evidence; and
(vii) Oral and written clarifications given by the Ministry to the points/issues raised by the
Members in the meeting of the Committee.
5. For facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the Committee
have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee, present this Twenty-first Report of the Committee relating to the Hire-Purchase 
(Amendment) Bill•, 1989. The Bill seeks to amend the Hire-Purchase Act , 1972. 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred•• the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya 
Sabha on the 5th May, 1989 and pending therein, to the Committee, for examination and 
report. 
3. The Committee considered the Bill and heard the representative of the Ministry of 
Law, Justice and Company Affairs in its meeting held on the 29th November, 1994. 
4. While considering the Bill, the Committee took note of the following documents/ 
information placed before it:-
(i) Background note on the Bill; 
(ii) Note explaining in chronological order the development from the enactment of 
the Hire Purchase Act, 1972 to the introduction of the Hire Purchase 
(Amendment) Bill, 1989; and 
(iii) Ninety-Second Report of the Committee on Petitions, Rajya Sabha relating to 
the question of bringing into force the Hire-Purchase Act , 1972. 
5. The Committee adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 19th July, 1995. 
6. From the information made available to the Committee and .the submission made by 
the representative of the Ministry, the Committee notes that the Hire-Purchase Act, 1972 
was enacted pursuant to the recommendations of the Law Commission contained in its 
Twentieth Report and the recommendations made by the Joint Committee of Parliament on 
the Hire Purchase Bill, 1968, mainly to regulate the hire-purchase transactions. befbre the 
Act could be enforced, several representations were received from various quarters against 
bringing the Act into force on account of certain difficulties/anomalies pointed out in its 
implementation. As a result of these representations, notifications giving effect to the Act 
had to be rescinded twice by the Government. The Committee on Petitions, Rajya Sabha, 
which had an occasion to examine the hire-Purchase Act, 1972, with particular reference to 
its non-enforcement, recommended that the Act be brought into force forthwith. It is in this 
back-drop that the Hire-Purchase (Amendment) Bill, 1989 was introduced in the Rajya 
Sabha on the 5th May, 1989 to overcome the main difficulties noticed. 
7. The Committee notes with serious concern that one of the reasons for non­
enforcement of the Hire Purchase Act, 1972 even after a lapse of 23 years was that no 
decision could be taken regarding the Ministry which would administer it. it is reall)' 
surprising that such a vital issue remained undecided for so long.

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee, present this Twenty-second Report . of the Committee relating to the 
Pondicherry (Administration) Amendment am·, 1995. The Bill seeks to insert a new section 
in the Pondicherry {Administration) Act, 1962 (49 of 1962), to make the provisions of 
Chapter VI of Part VI of the Constitution applicable to the High Court at Madras in relation 
to the exercise of its jurisdiction over the Union Territory of Pondicherry with effect from 
the 6th November, 1962. · 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred•• the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya 
Sabha on the 25th April, 1995 and pending therein, to the Committee, for examination and 
report. 
3. The Committee considered the ~ill in its meeting held on the 13th June, 1995 and also 
heard the representative of the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
4. The Committee while considering the Bill took note of the following documents 
furnished by the Ministry:-
(i) Background Note on "the Bill; 
(ii) The Pondieherry {Administration) Act, 1962 {49 fo 1962); and . . 
(iii) Relevant extracts from the Constitution. 
5. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 19th 
July, 1995. 
6. In its note fumished to the Committee, the Ministry explained the bactcground and the 
necessity for amendiag the Pondicherry {Administration) Act, 1962, as under:~ 
(i) Section 9 of Qte 'Act' provides tha~ as ft:om the sixth day of November, 1962, the 
jurisdiction of the 'High Court at Madras shall extend to the Union Territory of 
Pondicherry. 
(ii) Section 10 of the 'Act' provides inter-alia that the Madras High Court shall have, 
in respect of the Union Territory of Pondi~herry, all such jurisdiction, as under the 
law in force immediately before the appointed day (i.e. the 16th day of August, 1962) 
was exercisable in respect of French Establishment by the Cour de Cassation, the 
Cour Superieur d' Arbitrage and the Conseil d' Etat of France. However, the 'Act' 
does not expressly provide that the provisions of Chapter VI of Part VI of the 
Constitution shall be applicable .to the. High Court at Madras with respect to its 
administrative control over , the subordinate· coUrts in the Union Territory of 
Pondicherry. 
(iii') The necessity to amend the 'Act' arose as a result of Madras High Court 
judgement, and its subsequent endorsement by the Supreme Court, on certain writ

r the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Com~ittee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Twenty-third Report 
· of the Committee relating to the Arb itration and Conciliation Bill*, 1995. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred** the Arbitration and Conciliation Bill, 
l995, as introduced in the Ra jya Sabha on the 16th May, 1995 and pending therein , to the 
·Committee for examination and report. 
· · 3. The Committee, in its meeting held on the 17th August, 1995 considered the Bill and 
. . decided to invite the Law Secretary before it to make a presentation on the subject. 
Accordingly, the Law Secretary made a presentation on the Arbitration and Conciliation 
• Bill, 1995 before the Committee on the 4th September, 1995. During his presentation he 
explained the salient features of the Bill and the circumstances necessitating this 
comprehensive legislation. He infoni1ed the Committee that the present Legislations on the 
- subject, i.e. the Arbitration Act , 1940, the Arbitration (Protocol and Conventions) Act, 1937 
and the Foreign Awards (Recognition and Enforcement) Act, 1961 have become outdated. 
He stressed that economic reforms in the country may not become effective if the law 
dealing with settlement of domestic and international commercial disputes remains out of 
tune with such reforms. The Law Commission and several representative bodies of trade and 
industry have proposed amendments to the Arbitration Act of 1940. Further, the Law 
Secretaries and Law Ministers of all the States and Union Territories, at a meeting held at 
Calcutta on November 15- 17, 1994, also adopted a resolution that a comprehensive 
legislation on Arbitration and Conciliation be made, based largely on UNCITRAL Model 
Law. As explained in the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill, the General 
Assembly of the U.N. Commission on International Trade Law has also recommended that 
all the countries should give due consideration to the Model Law adopted by the U.N.O. 
The Law Secretary informed members that the proposed Bill seeks to consolidate and 
amend the Arbitration Law , taking into account the UNCITRAL Model Law and Rules . He 
also stated that a number of bodies/persons were consulted

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee, present this Twenty-fourth Report of the Committee relating to the Election 
Commission (Charging of Expenses on the Consolidated Fund of India) BiW, 1994. The Bill 
seeks to provide for charging of expenses of Election Commission on the Consolidated Fund 
of India. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha, 
referred•• the Bill, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 16th December, 1994 and pending 
therein, to the Committee, for examination and report. 
3.The Committee took up consideration of the Bill in its meeting held on the 13th 
March, 1995. It considered the Report in its meetings held on the 19th July and lOth 
November and adopted the same on the lOth November, 1995. In this connection, the 
Committee heard the representative of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs 
and considered the relevant information furnished by the Ministry including the extracts 
from the Constituent Assembly Debates regarding the views expressed therein on the 
question of making expenditure of the Election Commission 'charged' expenditure. 
4. From a perusal of the said debates, it appears that the Constituent Assembly, after 
due deliberations, in its wisdom decided that the expenditure of certain institutions/offices as 
mentioned in Article 112 of the Constitution, shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of 
India and thought it proper not ·to include the Election Commission therein. 
5. The representative of the Legislative Department of the Min.istry of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs also informed the Committee that the question of making the expenditure 
of Election Commission 'charged' expenditure was also considered in 1990 by a Committee 
headed by the then Law Minister Shri Dinesh Goswami. It did not think it necessary to 
make the expenditure of the Election Commission as 'charged' expenditure. The Goswami 
Committee was of the view that the expenditure of Election Commission should be 
continued as 'voted'. Hence, no recommendation was made by the said Committee to bring 
about any legislation in this regard.

Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby 
present this Two Hundred Forty Ninth  Report on Action Taken by Government on t he 
observations/recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Forty Second Report on Demands for 
Grants (2023-2024) of the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
 
2. The Two Hundred Forty Second Report of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Home Affairs was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 17 th March, 2023 and laid on the 
Table of the Lok Sabha on 20th March, 2023. After presentation of the Report, the copies thereof 
were sent to the Ministry of Home Affairs on 20 th March, 2023 requesting them to furnish Action 
Taken Notes on the recommendations of the Committee contained in the Report. The Ministry of 
Home Affairs furnished the Action Taken Notes on 30 st August, 2023 on the above mentioned Two 
Hundred Forty Second Report to the Committee.   
3. The Committee has noted that the statement on the status of implementation of the 
recommendations contained in the said Report of the Committee has not been laid on the Table of 
Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha in pursuant to the direction of Cha irman, Rajya Sabha dated                              
24th September 2004.

at its meeting held on 05th December, 2023.

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee , present this Twenty-fifth Report of the Committee relating to the Criminal Law 
(Second Amendment ) Bill, 1995•. The Bill seeks to further amend the Indian Penal Code 
1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure , 1973 and the Indian Evidence Act , 1872. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee , the Chairman , Rajya Sabha , in consultation with the Speaker , Lok Sabha , 
referred•• the Criminal Law (Second Amendment) Bill, 1995, as introduced in the Lok 
Sabha on the 21st August , 1995 and pending therein , to th e Committee for examination and 
report. 
3. The Committe e invited the Secretary , Ministry o f Home Affairs, to make a 
presentation on the various provisions of the Bill. Accordingly, he made a presentation 
before the Committee on the 21st November , 1995. During his presentation , he explained 
the salient features of the Bill and the circumstances necessitating the present legislation . 
4. The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its meeting held 
on the 22nd November , 1995. 
5. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 
4th December, 1995. 
6. The principal changes s uggested by the Committee in the Bill and the reasons 
therefor are set out hereinafter:-
Clause 2 
Clause 2 o f the Bill seeks to amend Section 220 of the Indian Penal Code, relating to 
punishment for corrupt or malicious commitment for trial or confinement by persons having 
authority. As stated in the Statement o f Objects and Reasons to the Bill, India became a 
signatory to t he Inte rnational Covenant on C ivil and Political Rights in 1979. Para 5 of

ii 
 
 
PREFACE 
 
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, 
having been authorized by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, do hereby present this Two 
Hundred Fifty Seventh Report on Demands for Grants (2026-27) relating to the Ministry of Home 
Affairs (MHA). 
2. Under Rule 272 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States, the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs is mandated to consider the 
Demands for Grants of the related Ministries and make report thereon. In pursuance thereof, the 
Committee in its meetings held on 16th and 17th February, 2026 heard the Home Secretary and other 
officers and considered the Demands for Grants (2026-27) of the Ministry of Home Affairs.  
3. The Committee in its sitting held on 16th March, 2026 considered and adopted the Report. 
4. The Committee while making its observations/recommendations has mainly relied upon the 
following documents:- 
 (i) Speech of Finance Minister on 1st February, 2026 while presenting the Union Budget 2026-
27; 
 (ii) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home Affairs for the year 2026-27; 
(iii) Output, Outcome, Monitoring framework of the Ministry 2026-27; 
(iv) Detailed Explanatory Notes on Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home Affairs for the 
year 2026-27; 
(v) Written replies furnished by the Ministry to the Questionnaires sent to them by the 
Secretariat;  
(vi) Presentations made by the Home Secretary and other concerned officers;  
(vii) Written clarifications furnished by the Ministry, on the points/issues raised by the Members 
during the deliberations of the Committee; and 
(viii) Verbatim transcripts of the meetings of the Committee held on 16th and 17th February, 
2026. 
 
5. For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee 
have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

REPORT 
I, the Chainnan of the Committee on Home AffairS, having been authorised by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, present this Twenty-seventh Report of the Committee, relating to the 
Private Security Guards and Agencies (Regulation) Bill, 1994* 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the 
Chainnan, Rajya Sabha referred** the Private Security Guards and Agencies (Regulation) Bill, 1994, as 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 14tli December, 1994 and pending therein, to the Committee for 
examination and report. 
3. With the increase in th~ number of business establishments, growth in crime rate and increasing de­
mands for surveillance, there has been a oroliferation of private security agencies in the recent years. There 
has also been a growing concern about the mann~r of functioning of these agencies. Unless suitable safe­
guards are devised, their activities are likely to have wide-ranging security implications, including the 
danger of their employees encroaching upon the duties of police. The Bill, therefore, seeks to regulate the 
private security agencies, by providing for a controlling authority to be appointed by the State Govern­
ments. 
4. The Committee invited the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs to make a presentation on various 
provisions of the Bill. Accordingly, he made a presentation before the Committee on the 21st November, 
1995. During his presentation he explained salient features of the Bill and the circumstances necessitating 
the present legislation. He infonned the Committee that at present there is no law to regulate the functioning 
of private security agencies. Hence, this proposed Bill. 
5. The Committee took-up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in its meeting held on the 29th 
January, 19% . 
6. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 9th February, 19%.

authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Third Report of the 
Committee.

Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred* the 
Supreme Court Judges (Conditions of Service) Amendment Bill**, 1991, as introduced in the Lok

and took up clause-by-clause consideration thereof.

Report. 
5. The Bill proposes to provide that where official residence is not provided to a Supreme Court 
Judge, he may be paid house rent allowance of Rs. 3000 per month which should be exempt from 
income tax. This provision is proposi!d to be given effect from the 9th May, 1986, when the number 
of Judges of the Supreme Court was increased and the official residence could not be provided 
immediately to some Judges. Accordingly, clauses 2 and 3 of the Bill were adopted by the Committee 
without any change. 
6. Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted with some changes which are of a 
consequential or drafting nature.

REPORT 
The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions was created as a separate 
Ministry from 1970 onwards in pursuance of the recommendations of the Administrative 
Reforms Commission (ARC). The ARC felt that the size of the Civil Services in the country 
warranted that a separate Ministry be created to deal with manifold problems which had 
emerged. However, the ARC recommended that this Ministry should always be under the 
charge of the Prime Minister. It was earlier created as a Department and in March, 1985 was 
constituted as a full-fledged Ministry. It is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister 
assisted by a Minister of State. The Ministry comprises the following three departments:-
(i) Department of Personnel and Training; 
(ii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances; 
(iii) Department of Pensions and Pensioners' Welfare. 
The three Departments function under Secretary (Personnel), assisted at present by 
three Additional Secretaries, four Joint Secretaries and other supporting officers and staff. 
2. The Department of Personnel and Training .also functions as the Administrative 
Ministry for the following agencies:-
(i) Central Bureau of Investigation· (CBI). (It is a premier investigative agency of the 
Government with Police powers, especially created to deal with corruptions related 
matters). 
(ii) Central Vigilance Commission (CVC). (Central agency to advise on all vigilance 
matters). 
(iii) Union Public Service Commission (UPSC). (A statutory body al}d recruitment 
Agency for Group 'A' and 'B' services/posts). 
(iv) Staff Selection Commission (SSC). (A recruitment agency for Group 'C' posts and 
also a few selected Group 'B' posts in the Central Secretariat). 
(v) Central Administrative Tribunals (CAl'). (A judicial body to provide justice to the 
Central Government employees in their service matters).

I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Thirty-fifth Report of the 
Committee, relating to the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 1996•. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha referred*" the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 1996, 
as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the lOth September, 1996 and pending therein. to the 
Committee for examination and report. 
3. The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill states that following suggestions from 
different fora and to take care of the changes which have taken place in the Capital market, 
operation of corporate sector and liberalisation policies. a need has been felt to undertake a 
comprehensive revision of the Companies Act. 1956 and accordingly Government has set up 
a Working Group to rewrite the Act. Since the whole exercise will take a considerable time 
to complete, some changes in the Act were felt imminent and therefore , this Bill. The Bill 
mainly seeks (i) to provide protection to the depositors; (ii) to provide protection to 
employees' interest in case of winding up of a Company; and (iii) to simplify some 
procedural and legal requirements in the interest of corporate sector. 
4. In its meeting held on the 8th October. 1996 the Committee heard the Secretary, 
Legislative· Department on various aspects of the Bill, but deferred his further evidence till 
the representative of the Department of Company Affairs which was the administrative 
Ministry concerned with the Bill appeared before it and explained the nature of the 
proposed amendments and their broad thrust. 
5. In its meeting held on the 9th October, 1996 the Committee heard the representative 
of the Department of Company Affairs on the salient features of the Bill and the urgency of 
the Bill pending the comprehensive redrafting of the entire Companies Act currently in 
progress. In the course of his presentation, the Committee was informed about the 
composition of the Working Group which has been assigned with the task of redrafting the 
Companies Act. The Committee expressed its displeasure over the composition of the 
working group as it was not broad ba~ed and representative in character in that the investors 
and the representatives of Industry and institutions like Institute of Chartered Accountants 
of India, Institute of Cost and Works. Accountants of India , institute of Company Secretaries 
of India etc. had not been given adequate representation . The Committee strongly feels that 
the Working Group be expanded so as to include official representatives of the said 
organisations/institutions formally sponsored by them and well known experts in. the related 
fields so that it inspires greater confidence in the minds of the public. 
6. In its sitting held on the 23rd October, 1996. the Committee took up clause-by-clause 
consideration of the Bill.

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Fortieth Report of the 
Committee, relating to the Lokpal Bill, 1996*. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha 
referred** the Lokpal Bill, 1996, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on the 13th September, 
1996 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and Report. 
3. The institution of Lokpal, as the Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the 
Bill says, has been sought to be established on the basis of the recommendations of the 
Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) contained in its interim Report on the 
"Problem of Redress of Citizens' Grievances". This Report of the ARC was submitted in 
1966 and the earlier attempts at legislation for setting up such an institution could not 
fructify in 1968, 1971, 1977, 1985 and 1989 for various reasons. The current Bill, as the 
Statement of Objects and Reasons goes on to say, seeks to carry out the object and purpose 
of the recommendations 'of ARC for enabling the citizens to have recourse to a convenient 
and effective forum for determination of complaints and thereby save him from pursuing his 
remedy through the process of Courts, which may prove to be expertsive or dilatory and may 
not facilitate speedy determination. 
4. The concept of having an institution like the Lokpal arises from the need for 
redressal of citizens' grievances. The term Lokpal is akin to the English term 'Ombudsman' 
which has been described in Chamber's Dictionary as a 'grievance man'. Ombudsman means 
an official who is appointed to investigate complaints against the administration. In other 
woi'Qs, Ombudsman is an officer who investigates complaints of citizens of unfair treatment 
meted out to them by Government Departments and suggests remedy thereof, if he finds 
that a complaint is justified. The institution of Ombudsman came into being in 1713 in 
Sweden when Chancellor of justice was appointed by the King to act as an invigilator to look 
into the functioning of the war time Government. In the year 1809, provision was made for 
the appointment of Ombudsman by the legislature. The institution remained mainly confined 
to the Scandinavian countries such as Finland and Denmark, In 1962 New Zealand also 
adopted the system of Ombudsman. Great Britain also did not lag behind

do hereby present this Forty-third Report on the Demands for Grants (1998-99) relating to

2. The Committee held in all five sittings to complete the examination of the Demands

and heard the Secretary of the Ministry. In its meeting held on 23rd June, 1998 the 
Committee heard DirC?ctors-General of ITBP, BSF and CRPF on the Demands relating to 
their respective forces. The Committee again heard the Secretary in its meeting held on the

Commissioner of Police, Delhi, on Demands relating to Delhi Police. 
3. The Committee while makir.g its observations/recommendations ·has mainly relied 
upon the following :

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Forty-ninth Report of the 
Committee on the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1997*. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Presiding Officer, Rajya Sabha referred**. The Code of Civil Procedure 
(Amendment) Bill, 1997 as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 14th August, 1997 and 
pending therein, to the earlier Committee (1997-98) for examination and report . 
3. The Committee (1997-98) considered the Bill in its meeting held on 30th September, 
1997 and heard the Secretary of the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs on the provisions contained in the Bill. 
4. In the said meeting of the Committee, having regard to the special importance of the 
Bill which sought to streamline the procedural delays in the judicial process a~d amend 
certain Sections and Orders of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, decided to invite 
memoranda from individuals/organisations/ins titutions etc. interested in the subject matter 
of Bill. The Committee directed that a Press Communique may be issued in this behalf 
fixing November 10, 1997 as the last date for the receipt of memoranda. An advertisement 
was, accordingly, published in all the leading English and Vernacular dailies on 11th 
October, 1997. The matter was also broadcast/telecast repeatedly on All India Radio and 
Doordarshan to give it wide publicity. 
S. Since the intended amendments were of far-reaching importance to the .community of 
lawyers and litigants and would have a significant impact on the administration of justice, it 
was also decided to .invite views/suggestions from the Bar Council of India, State Bar 
Councils and Bar Associations of Allahabad, Bombay, Calcutta , Delhi, Guwahati, Kerala, 
Madras and two District Bar Associations from each S tate. Accordingly, !hey were 
requested to send their views/suggestions on the Bill. 
6. Before the Committee (1997-98) could proceed further with the consideration of the 
Bill, it got dissolved consequent upon the dissolution of the Eleventh Lok Sabha on 
4.12.1997.

2. In pursuanr.:e of the rules relating to the Department-Related Parliamentary 
Standing Committees , the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker , 
Lok Sabha, referred '" The Census (Amendment) Bill, 1992**, as introduced in the Lok 
Sabha on the 18th December, 1992 and pending in that House , to the Committee for 
examination and report. 
3. The Committee in its meeti ngs held on the 18th, 19th and 25th August, 1993 
discussed the provisions of the Bill and also heard the views of the represe:ntative s of 
the Ministries of Home Affairs and Law , Justice & Company Affairs. In its meeting 
held on the 25th August , 1993, the Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration 
of the Bill. 
In the said meeting the Committee considered and adopted the drafl Report. 
4. ln their background note supplied to the Committee, the Ministry of Home Affair~ 
explained the need for amending the Census At"t, 1948 as follows:-
'The Census is normally taken after every 10 years. The last Census being held in 
1991, the next decennial census would lake place in the year 2001 only. However . 
the Census Organisation is required to undertake surveys or census in parts of the 
country from time to time meet the exigencies of the situation. for example, an 
ethographic survey was done in Jammu & Kashmir in the year 1986-87 to identify 
the communities which should be declared as Scheduled Tribe s. Similarly, in 
Punjab, a survey was done in Kandu Khera village in the year 1986. That is, under 
the Census Act, 1948, census can be taken in any part of the country at any 
particular point of time. Accordingly , it is necessary to get the Census (Amend­
ment) Bill passed as quickly as possible to meet such emergent situations. 
Under the Census (Amendment) Bill, powers are being vested with the Central 
Government to determine the question .naire s for the Census. This power was 
earlier vested with the State Governments ... Different State Governments followed 
different approaches. This not only created administrative difficulties but also, due 
to lack of uniformity, led to uneven quality of data. However , the situation has 
changed drastically in the country during the last three or four decades and it is 
essentia l that there should be uniformity of norms and standards, etc. in the 
censuses and surveys throughout the country. It is towards this end that the powers 
to determine the census questionnaires are being vested with the Central 
Government under the Census (Amendment) Bill ...

1, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Home Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this Fifty-third Report of the Committe~. The Report is on the Immigration 
(Carriers' Liability) Bill, 1998. • 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha 
referred** the Immigration (Carriers' Liability) Bill, 1998 as introduced in the Rajya Sabha 
on the 23rd December, 1998 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and 
report. 
3. The Bill intends to make the carriers liable in respect of passengers brought by them 
into India in contrav entio n of the provisions of the Passport (Entry into India) Act , 1920, 
and the Passport (Entry into India) Rules, 1950. The said Act and the 'rules made. 
thereunder prescribe the conditions for the entry of a person' coming from any place outside 
India by water, land or air. Under these rules, foreign nationals are required to be in 
possession of a valid passport and a visa. An Indian national must be in possession of a valid 1 
passport. The Immigration authorities posted at various checkposts covering land checkposts, 
seaports and airport s are required to do a thorough checking of the persons coming by 
different mpdes of transport. 
4. The Ministry of Home Affairs in their Background Note on the Bill has stated that it 
has been observed in recent years that a large number of passengers at the four major 
Internat ional airports at Delhi, Bombay , Calcutta and Madras manage to come without any 
valid documents, creat ing problems for the immigration authorities. Airlines do not exercise 
proper check of travel documents before allowing passengers to board the plane. It has, 
therefore, become nece~sary that stat utory responsibility is cast on the airlines/ship carriers 
bringing such passengers by imposing financial liability on them, states, the Ministry in their 
Note.· 
5. International air travel is governed by the guidelines adopted at the Convention on 
Internatinal Civil Aviation signed at Chicago on December 7, 1944, known as the Chicago 
Convention. It has various annexures finalised over a period of time during the last 50 years.

functioning under the Cabinet Secretary had an important role to play in the senior appointments under the Government

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
 
RAJYA SABHA
DEPARTMENT-RELATED PARLIAMENTARY
STANDING COMMITTEE ON HOME AFFAIRS
SEVENTY FOURTH REPORT
ON
 
THE CONSTITUTION (NINETY-FIRST AMENDMENT) BILL, 2000
 
(PRESENTED TO RAJYA SABHA ON 26th APRIL, 2001)
(LAID ON THE TABLE LOK SABHA ON 26th APRIL, 2001)
 
REPORT
            The Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Bill, 2000 (See Annexure-I) seeks to amend altogether six Articles of the
Constitution (55, 81, 82, 170, 330 and 332) to remove the distortions and disparities caused due to uneven growth of
population/electorate in territorial constituencies for Lok Sabha/Legislative Assemblies, while sustaining the measure to boost
family planning norms.
1.1              To achieve the foresaid objective, the Bill has the following enabling provisions:-
(i)                  extending the constitutional embargo on undertaking fresh delimitation of constituencies from the year 2000 to
2026;
(ii)                readjustment and rationalization of Parliamentary constituencies in the States without altering the number of seats
allotted to each State in the House of People, including the Schedule Caste and the Scheduled Tribe constituencies,
on the basis of 1991 population census;
(iii)               readjustment and rationalization of Assembly constituencies in the States without altering the number of seats
allotted to each State in their Legislative Assemblies, including the Scheduled Caste and the Scheduled Tribe
constituencies, on the basis of 1991 population census; and
(iv)              refixing the number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the House of the
People and the Legislative Assemblies of the States on the basis of 1991 population census.
2.0       The amendment to the aforesaid seven Articles has been necessitated mainly due to the following two facts:-
(i)                  the constitutional embargo on the delimitation of territorial constituencies (both Parliamentary and Assembly),
imposed by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, will expire after the publication of first census
after the year 2000 AD, the process of which has already been set in motion; and
(ii)
                the growth of population is not uniform in the country.  The unbalanced and uneven growth of population as well
as continuous migration of people from one place to another, especially from rural to urban areas have resulted in
strikingly different sizes of electoral constituencies even within the State.  The most glaring example is outer Delhi
Parliamentary constituency, which had approximately 29.3 lakhs population whereas the Chandni Chowk
Parliamentary Constituency had a population of 3.7 lakhs (both 1998 figures).
2.1       The last delimitation of territorial constituencies was done on the basis of decennial population census of 1971 by the
Delimitation Commission, constituted for the purpose by the Delimitation Act, 1972 (See Annexure-II).  The Commission took
roughly four years to complete the delimitation work on that occasion, after which the delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly
Constituencies Order, 1976 came into force. 
2.1.1    The ban on the delimitation was imposed by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment)Act, 1976 with a specific aim to
boost family planning norms.  It was thought at that time that the States which did not control their population should not get
rewarded through the delimitation process and that by the year, 2000, the progress of implementation of family planning would,
more or less be uniform throughout the country.
2.1.2    But it is found that the population growth since 1971 census is quite haphazard and uneven.  The said uneven growth is

74th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/74threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:40:50]
attributed mainly to the fact that some States have gone slow in arresting population explosion whereas some States especially
those in the South have achieved  comparative success in the implementation of family planning programme.
2.1.3    Delimitation on the basis of 2001 population census, in effect, would mean that States which are successful in arresting
population growth to a large extent, would be in disadvantageous position vis-à-vis the States which have gone slow in the
implementation of family planning programme, in the inter-State allocation of seats in the House of the People.
2.2.0    Keeping in view the rationale narrated in the previous para, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has recommended
(See Annexure-III) extending the current freeze up to the year 2026  as by that time the replacement level of fertility would be
expected to be achieved at national level.  In other words, the population growth in the country would be comparatively even by
the year 2026.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been
authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Ninety-fifth Report of the
Committee on the Repatriation of Prisoners Bill, 2002.
2.         In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred ** the Repatriation of Prisoners Bill, 2002 as
introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 9 May 2002 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
 
3.         The Committee considered the Bill in its sittings held on 3 July, 9 September and 9 October 2002.
 
3.1       The Committee took oral evidence of the Special Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs in its sitting held on 3
July 2002.
 
3.2       In its sitting held on 9 September 2002, the Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.
 
3.3       The Committee considered the draft Report on the Bill and adopted the same in its sitting held on 9 October
2002.

having been authorized by the Committee to submit t he Report on their behalf, present 
the Thirty-First Report on the subject “Functioning  of Delhi Development Authority 
particularly with reference to Affordable Houses in  Delhi and its Role in Regularization 
of Unauthorized Colonies in Delhi and matter connec ted thereto” relating to the Ministry 
of 
 Urban Development.  
 
2. The Committee took the oral-evidence of the repr esentatives  of the Ministry of  
Urban Development, DDA, NDMC, MCD and Registrar Co- operative Societies of 
Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi ( GNCTD) on 21 st  January, 2013, 8 th  & 
31 st  October,2013, 6 th  November, 2013 and 12 th  February, 2014. The Committee also 
took oral evidence of Shri Sandeep Dixit, MP, LS on 7 th  February, 2013. The Committee 
also heard the view-points of Shri Mahabal Mishra, MP, LS, and representatives of 
Resident Welfare Associations of various colonies in Delhi on 6 th  November, 2013. 
3. The Committee considered and adopted the report at their sitting held on        
12 th  March, 2014. 
4. The Committee wish to express their thanks to th e Officers of Ministry of Urban 
Development and DDA, NDMC, MCD and Registrar Co-ope rative Societies of 
Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi ( GNCTD) for furnishing the material 
and information which the Committee desired from ti me to time  in connection with the 
examination of the subject and also for  appearing before the  Committee.

Mishra, MPs, LS and the representatives of Resident  Welfare Associations (RWAs) of 
various colonies for  sharing their views and sugge stions and also for  appearing before 
the Committee.

the Committee have been printed in bold letters in part II of the Report.

INTRODUCTION 
  
 I, the Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Urban Development (2014 -15) 
(Sixteenth Lok Sabha) having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report 
on their behalf, present the First Report on Demands for Grants (2014 -15) of the 
Ministry of Urban Development. 
2. The Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Urban Development were laid on the 
table of the House on 13 th August, 2014. Under Rule 331E of the Rules of Procedure 
and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, the Standing Committee on Urban 
Development are required to consid er the Demands for Grants of the Ministries under 
their jurisdiction and make Report on the same to both the Houses of Parliament. 
Thereafter, the Demands are considered by the House in the light of the Report of the 
Committee. However, during the current year, being election year, the demands were 
passed by both the Houses of Parliament without subjecting them to examination by the 
DRSCs. As per directions of the Hon'ble Speaker, the demands have been examined by 
the Committee and reported upon with the in tention that the recommendations of the 
Committee can be utilised by the Ministry for future Demands for Grants. 
3. The Committee took evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of Urban 
Development on 17th October, 2014. The Committee wish to express  their thanks to the 
officials of the Ministry of Urban Development for placing before them the requisite 
material and their considered views in connection with the examination of the Demands 
for Grants (2014-15). 
4. The Committee considered  and adopted th e Report at their sitting held on 12 
December, 2014.

have been printed in bold letters and placed as Part II of the report.

INTRODUCTION   
 I, the Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Urban Development (2014-15) (Sixteenth 
Lok Sabha) having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on their behalf, 
present the Second Report on Demands for Grants (201 4-15) of the Ministry of Housing and 
Urban Poverty Alleviation.  
 
2. The Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation were 
laid on the table of the House on 13 th August, 2014. Under Rule 331E of the Rules of Procedure 
and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, the Standing Co mmittee on Urban Development are 
required to consider the Demands for Grants of the Ministries under their jurisdiction and make 
Report on the same to both the Houses of Parliament. Thereafter, the Demands are considered 
by the House in the light of the Re port of the Committee. However, during the current year, being 
election year, the Demands  were passed by both the Houses of Parliament without subjecting 
them to examination by the DRSCs. As per directions of the Hon'ble Speaker, the demands have 
been examined by the Committee and reported upon with the intention that the recommendations 
of the Committee can be utilised by the Ministry for future Demands for Grants. 
 
3. The Committee took evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of Housing and Urban  
Poverty Alleviation on 25 th September, 2014. The Committee wish to express their thanks to the 
officials of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation for placing before them the 
requisite material and their considered views in connection with the examination of the Demands 
for Grants (2014-15).

PART-I 
CHAPTER- I 
INTRODUCTORY 
 
 (i) Role of the Ministry  
1.1 The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) is entrusted with 
the responsibility of broad policy formulation and monitoring of programmes 
regarding urban housing and urban development. It is the nodal Ministry for 
planning and coordination of urban transport matters at the central level. 
Urban devel opment is a State subject and the Constitution (Seventy -
Fourth) Amendment Act, 1992 has enjoined upon State Governments to 
delegate many functions to urban local bodies.  Government of India, 
however, plays a coordinating and monitoring role and also suppo rts 
various urban housing programmes, urban livelihood mission and overall 
urban development through Central and Centrally Sponsored Schemes. 
The Ministry addresses various issues relevant to urban sector through 
appropriate policy guidelines, subordinate legislation and sectoral 
programmes. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs has f ive attached 
Offices, and three Subordinate Offices, three Public Sector Undertaking s 
and nine Statutory/Autonomous Bodies, including one non -statutory 
registered society and a Government company as shown at Annexure-I.  
 Background 
1.2 Outlining the transformation from rural to urban areas witnessed in 
the country during the last two decades and future requirements to cater to 
ever increasing urban population , the Secretary,(MoHUA) during the 
course of briefing submitted: 
“महोदय , आपने संक्षेप में शुरुआती जो व्याख्यान ददया  है, उसमें आपने बताया 
है दि दिस प्रिार से हमारे देश  में शहरी दििास एि बहुत बड़ी चुनौती िे तौर 

2 
 
पर आगे आ रहा है। दजस प्रिार से शहरों िी आबादी  बढ़ रही है, अगर हम िर्ष 
2001 िे बाद  िर्ष 2011 िे शहरों िी आबादी  देखें  तो उसमें दजस तरह से 
बढ़ोतरी हुई है और जो आगे बढ़ने िा अनुमान है, िर्ष 2011 िी जनगणना िे 
अनुसार शहरी इलािों िी आबादी  िरीब 38 िरोड़ िी थी। इसिा अनुमान है 
दि लगभग  40 परसेंट पॉपुलेशन  यानी हमारी आबादी  60 िरोड़ से ज्यादा िर्ष 
2030 में हो जाएगी। जब िर्ष 2031 िा सेंसस होगा और िर्ष 2051 िी जो 
जनगणना होगी, तब हमारी आबादी  80 िरोड़ से िहीं ज्यादा हो जाएगी, जो 
दि देश  िे 50 परसेंट से ज्यादा यानी हम लोग  आज िी डेट में जो ग्रामीण 
प्रधान देश  िहते हैं, उसिी जगह हम शहरी प्रधान देश  िर्ष 2051 िी 
जनगणना िे बाद  हो जाएँगे। 
सर, शहर हमारे दलए  एि तरफ तो चुनौती लाता  है, उसि े आधारभूत संरचना 
िे बारे में, जैसा आपने िहा सेदनटेशन िे बारे में, िाटर िे बारे में, सीिर 
दसस्टम िे बारे में, दबजली  िे बारे में, क्ोंदि ये तमाम सारे लोग  एि जगह पर 
इिट्ठा होते हैं, उनिो िे तमाम सारी आधारभूत सुदिधाएँ देनी  पड़ती हैं, दजससे 
हम िह िातािरण दिएट िर सि ें, दजससे िे अपनी आदथषि गदतदिदधयों िो 
पूरा िरते हुए देश  िी अथषव्यिस्था में पूरा योगदान  दे  सि ें । 
सर, आज शहरों िा जीडीपी में लगभग  60 प्रदतशत िा योगदान  है। आज 
हमारा जो टोटल  रेिेन्यू है, िह 80 परसेंट से ज्यादा शहरी इलािों से आता है। 
माननीय प्रधान मंत्री जी ने आज देश  िे दििास िे दलए  थ्री दटिदलयन डालर 
इिोनॉमी िो फाइि दटिदलयन डालर इिोनॉमी िर्ष 2024 ति िरने और िर्ष 
2030 ति 10 दटिदलयन डालर इिोनॉमी बनाने िी जो एि चुनौती ली  है, मैं 
समझता हँ दि शहरों िा इसमें बहुत बड़ा योगदान  होगा। मैं आपिो यह भी 
िहना चाहँगा दि िर्ष 2014 िे बाद  से शहरों िे दििास में अभूतपूिष तेजी आई 
है। िर्ष 2014 ति दजस प्रिार से माननीय प्रधान मंत्री जी ने एि िे बाद  एि 
दमशन अप्रोच में बहुत सारी योजनाएँ हमारे मंत्रालय िे दलए  भारत सरिार ने 
स्वीि ृ त िीं और उन योजनाओं िा जो पररणाम सामने आ रहा है, िह उसि े 
दलए  चुनौती है, लेदिन चुनौती िो हम लोग  पूरा िरने िे दलए  एि तरीि े से 
उस रास्ते पर हैं दि ि ै से इसिो पूरा िर सिते हैं।“

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Housing and Urban Affairs (2023-24) having been 
authorized by the Committee, present this Twentieth Report (1 7th Lok Sabha) on action taken by the 
Government on the Observations/Recommendations contained in the Seventeenth Report (17th Lok Sabha) 
of the Committee on the subject, ‘Evaluation of Implementation of Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban). 
2. The Seventeenth Report was presented to Lok Sabha on 20 March 2023 but had been laid on the 
table of Rajya Sabha on 17 March 2023 . The Action Taken Replies of the Government to all the 
recommendations contained in the Report were received on 18 August, 2023. 
3. The Committee considered and adopted this Report at their sitting held on 31st October, 2023. 
4. An analysis of the action taken by the Government on the  recommendations contained in the 
Seventeenth Report (Seventeenth Lok Sabha) of the Committee is given at Annexure-II. 
5. For the facility of  reference and convenience, the Observations/Recommendations of the 
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

INTRODUCTION 
 I, the Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Housing and Urban Affairs 
(2024-25) having been authorized by the Committee, present this Second Report  
(18th Lok Sabha) on action taken by the Government on the 
Observations/Recommendations contained in the Twenty First Report (17th Lok Sabha) 
of the Committee on the subject, ‘Smart Cities Mission: An Evaluation’ of the Ministry of 
Housing and Urban Affairs’. 
2. The Twenty First Report was presented to Lok Sabha on 08.02.2024 and laid on 
the table of Rajya Sabha on the same date. The Action Taken Replies of the 
Government to all the recommendations contained in the Report were received on  
19 July 2024. 
3. The Committee considered and adopted this Report at their sitting held on  
05th December, 2024. 
4. An analysis of the action taken by the Government on the recommendations 
contained in the Twenty First Report (Seventeenth Lok Sabha) of the Committee is 
given at Annexure-II. 
5. For the facility of reference and convenience, the 
Observations/Recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters in 
the body of the Report.

CHAPTER–I
MEMORANDUM  OF  UNDERSTANDING  BETWEEN  FERTILIZER  PSUS  AND DEPARTMENT  OF 
FERTILIZERS
1.1       The commitments and mutual responsibilities of the Government and the PSUs are clearly defined in the MoU
System. The targets are finalised at the beginning of the year and so are the commitments of the Department of
Fertilizers. The evaluation of the performance of these targets is carried out only at the end of the year. The focus under
the MoU system hence is said to have shifted from mere input orientation to result orientation. This also envisages a
system granting more autonomy to the PSUs with lesser involvement of the Ministries and Departments in the control of
the day-to-day functioning of the PSUs through laid down procedures etc.
1.2       The Sub-Committee-III on Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises of Department-related Parliamentary Standing

public sector Company after the take over of the erstwhile Metal Corporation of India Limited, to develop mining and
smelting capacities to meet the domestic demand of zinc and lead metals. The Government held 75.92% of the equity as
24.08% of its equity was disinvested during the period 1991-93.  Government decided to further disinvest 26% equity

disinvested 26% equity of HZL and management of the company has been transferred to the Strategic Partner  (S.P.)
namely, M/s Sterlite Opportunities and Ventures Ltd. with this  disinvestment the stake  of the Government in the
Company has come down    to 49.92% .

CHAPTER–I
LIQUIDATED DAMAGES – THE CONCEPT
            In a supply contract if there is a delay beyond the contractual delivery period in execution of supply, services,
erection and commissioning, the consignee may end up suffering actual or potential losses. Direct losses arising out of
the delay actual in nature that can be directly quantified like debt servicing etc. Potential losses are indirect losses like
opportunity costs, cost overrun of the project, time overrun of the project leading to inflation of project cost etc. The
losses tantamount to the damages suffered by the consignee and quantified unit of these damages are known as
Liquidated Damages.
2.         As per the standard terms of conditions of contracts internationally acclaimed the amount of liquidated damages
is generally ½% of the total value of the contract for every week of delay in supplies or other performance of the
contract plus any cost escalation that has taken place on account of any increase in taxes or imposition of fresh taxes, or
cost escalation of any raw material on account of this during the period of delay, cost escalation of labour due to any
new wage agreement, or imposition of any statutory conditions. However, the supplier will be entitled to any decrease in
cost on the above account of remission of taxes or withdrawal of taxes during the said period between

1.1     The Ministry of Small Scale Industries is the nodal Ministry for policy formulation, promotion, development and
protection of Small Scale Industries. It also monitors the implementation of these policies.
1.2     Ministry of SSI designs and implements the policies through its field organizations for promotion and growth of
small enterprises. The Ministry also coordinates with other Ministries/Departments on behalf of the Small Scale
Industries (SSI) sector.
1.3     Implementation of policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure and support services to
small enterprises is undertaken through its attached office, namely the Small Industries Development Organization
(SIDO).
1.4     The Indian economy has experienced profound changes and sustained growth in the last five decades. Industry
sector, by building core strength of the economy, has acted as an engine of growth. The Small Scale Industries (SSI)
sector has also contributed significantly in process of growth and has emerged as a vibrant partner. The importance of
the sector can be well assessed in terms of its contribution to the socio-economic objectives of growth in generation of
employment, output, exports.
1.5     The SSI sector, producing a wide range of products, accounts for around 95 per cent of the industrial units in the
country, contributing to 40 per cent of the manufacturing sector output and approximately one-third of the Nation's

REPORT
 
        The Department of Public Enterprises acts as a nodal agency for all PSEs and assists in policy formulation
pertaining to the policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, financial accounting, personnel
management and in related areas. It also collects, evaluates and maintains information on several areas in respect of

1.1   The important role and tasks of the Department of Public Enterprises are :

1.         The Department of Heavy Industry (Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises) is responsible for promoting
engineering industry in the country and development and growth of capital goods.  The industries covered by this Department
provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport. They also cater to the
requirements of equipment for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping,
paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for the development of  wide range of intermediate engineering
products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gearboxes.  There are 49  Public  Sector Enterprises (PSEs)
under the administrative charge of the Department.
1.1       The PSEs under the administrative control of the Department are engaged in manufacturing of engineering/capital goods,
consultancy and contracting activities. The total investment (Gross Block) in 49 Public Sector Enterprises under the Department
of Heavy Industry was about Rs.8234.00 crores till 31st March, 2002,  employing about 1.18  lakh persons.

CHAPTER - I 
MOU SYSTEM 
1.         The Memorandum of Undertaking (MOU)  is a negotia ted document between the Government, acting as the owner of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific
PSE. It contain the intentions, obligations and mutual responsib ilities of the Government and the PSE. Further, MOU makes an at tempt to move the management of PSEs
from management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.  
OBJECTIVES OF THE MOU SYSTEM  
1.1       The objectives of the MOU system are to improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy and accountability of the management; to remove the
fuzziness in the goals and objectives of the enterprise  to pursue through clearly laid down performance targets   in the  MOU and to enable the evaluation of managerial
performance through objective criteria and provide a mechanism to reward good performance through performance incentives to stimulate improved performance.

management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.

CHAPTER - I
IMPACT  OF  FISCAL  POLICY  AND  EXIM POLICY  ON  CAPITAL  GOODS  INDUSTRIES
        In early eighties, when India's economy was on an uptrend, there was need for investment in the infrastructure sector.
Investment from within India was not forthcoming mainly because of higher rate of interest and private sector risk aversions.
Investment during those years was mainly from multilateral/bilateral funding agencies. For judicious usage of these funds, the
projects were established under International Competitive Bidding procedures. Indian companies were also eligible to participate
in the bidding procedure. Overseas suppliers could enjoy soft export financing from their exim banking and other export benefits
prevailing in those countries. The Indian companies were also extended the duty free raw material imports and refund of excise
duty on their finished goods to have a level playing field. Supplies to such projects were termed as Deemed Exports.
        As a part of the commitment given to WTO, the peak rate of customs duty was to be brought down to a level agreed with
WTO in a time bound matter and accordingly the rate of customs duty for the project was also reduced gradually. Project import

of the Small Scale Sectors- including the Problems in Procurement of Raw Material”.   However, the Committee
decided to consider the Problems being faced by SSI units in the procurement of  steel as an urgent issue.

interacted with the representatives of the Ministry of Steel and the Ministry of Small Scale Industries.   The present
report has been prepared  taking into account the background note furnished by the Ministry of Steel and the Ministry of
SSI and the suggestions which emerged during the  interaction with the SSI Associations.

CHAPTER-I
 
THE STEEL SECTOR
1.1       Steel is crucial to the development of any modern economy. It has  technologically strong forward and backward
linkages in terms of material flow and income generation.   The growth of  many of  advanced economies have been
largely shaped by the strength of their steel industry during their early stages of development.    Some of the newly
industrializing  countries like South Korea, China and Brazil among others have built up substantial capacities not only
to support their rapidly growing domestic economies, but also to export significantly.
